text: Andreas Speiser (June 10, 1885 – October 12, 1970) was a Swiss mathematician and philosopher of science. He studied in Göttingen beginning in 1904, under prominent figures including David Hilbert, Felix Klein, and Hermann Minkowski. In 1917, he became a full-time professor at the University of Zurich, later moving to Basel. During 1924/25, he served as president of the Swiss Mathematical Association. His research focused on number theory, group theory, and the theory of Riemann surfaces. He organized the translation of Leonard Dickson's 1923 book Algebras and Their Arithmetics, published in German as Algebren und ihre Zahlentheorie in 1927, a work significantly influenced by the algebraic research of Emmy Noether and Helmut Hasse; Speiser also contributed an appendix on ideal theory to the book. His book Theorie der Gruppen endlicher Ordnung is a classic, richly illustrated treatise on group theory, featuring applications in Galois theory, elementary number theory, and the study of Platonic solids, as well as detailed analyses of ornaments, which he examined during a 1928 trip to Egypt. Speiser made contributions to the history of mathematics, serving as chief editor for the Euler Commission's edition of Leonhard Euler's Opera Omnia and as editor of the works of Johann Heinrich Lambert. As a philosopher, he primarily focused on Plato, writing a commentary on the Parmenides Dialogue, and was also an expert in the philosophies of Plotinus and Hegel. His doctoral students included J. J. Burckhardt.
